case_info.scenario: A 38-year-old man presented for evaluation of lesions on his elbows for 10 years, hands for 1 year, and knees for a few months. The lesions were progressively increasing in number and size and were occasionally mildly tender with firm pressure. He was unaware of similar lesions or known lipid abnormalities in family members. Physical examination revealed numerous pink-yellow firm papules and nodules on the bilateral elbows (Figure 1A) and knees, and linear thin yellow papules on the palmar finger creases. A shave biopsy specimen was taken from a papule on the elbow and sent for histopathologic analysis (Figure 1B). A fasting serum lipid panel was also obtained. Based on the clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings, the patient was diagnosed with an underlying genetic disorder.
case_info.caption: Clinical image of right elbow shows numerous pink-yellow firm papules and nodules (A), and hematoxylin-eosin staining (original magnification, ×200) of shave biopsy specimen shows sheets of foamy lipid-filled histiocytes (B).
case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

4. Frustration
   Definition:

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

The lesions were progressively increasing in number and size and were occasionally mildly tender with firm pressure. He was unaware of similar lesions or known lipid abnormalities in family members. case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 38-year-old man presented for evaluation of lesions on his elbows for 10 years, hands for 1 year, and knees for a few months. The lesions were progressively increasing in number and size and were occasionally mildly tender with firm pressure. He was unaware of similar lesions or known lipid abnormalities in family members. Physical examination revealed numerous pink-yellow firm papules and nodules on the bilateral elbows (Figure 1A) and knees, and linear thin yellow papules on the palmar finger creases. A shave biopsy specimen was taken from a papule on the elbow and sent for histopathologic analysis (Figure 1B). A fasting serum lipid panel was also obtained. Based on the clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings, the patient was diagnosed with an underlying genetic disorder.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The tender nature of the lesions and their distribution further supports this diagnosis, as they often correlate with a lipid disorder.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 38-year-old man presented for evaluation of lesions on his elbows for 10 years, hands for 1 year, and knees for a few months. The lesions were progressively increasing in number and size and were occasionally mildly tender with firm pressure. He was unaware of similar lesions or known lipid abnormalities in family members. Physical examination revealed numerous pink-yellow firm papules and nodules on the bilateral elbows (Figure 1A) and knees, and linear thin yellow papules on the palmar finger creases. A shave biopsy specimen was taken from a papule on the elbow and sent for histopathologic analysis (Figure 1B). A fasting serum lipid panel was also obtained. Based on the clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings, the patient was diagnosed with an underlying genetic disorder.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",

    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",

    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 13.3. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

The lesions were progressively increasing in number and size and were occasionally mildly tender with firm pressure. He was unaware of similar lesions or known lipid abnormalities in family members. case_info.explanation: A. Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) Histopathologic findings showed aggregates of lipid-filled histiocytes, consistent with xanthoma. The patient’s distribution of lesions was consistent with xanthoma striatum palmare, tuberous xanthomas, and tuberoeruptive xanthomas, suggestive of an underlying diagnosis of familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (FD). Lipid profiling revealed elevated cholesterol (519 mg/dL; normal range, <200 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0259), elevated triglycerides (935 mg/dL; normal range, <150 mg/dL; for mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113), and reduced high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (22 mg/dL; normal range, 40-60 mg/dL). Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol could not be calculated due to the high triglyceride levels. Altogether, the patient’s clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings confirmed the diagnosis of FD. He declined genetic testing. Statin therapy was initiated, and after 1 year of treatment, most of the lesions had completely disappeared. Despite being benign, xanthomas often herald underlying lipid metabolism disorders. Xanthomas are classified based on clinical morphologic findings, anatomic distribution, and mode of development, and include tendon, planar, tuberous, tuberoeruptive, and eruptive xanthomas.1Histologically, all xanthoma types are characterized by a dense collection of foam cells (histiocytes filled with lipid) within the dermis. Eruptive xanthomas often contain extracellular lipid and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate, whereas tuberous and tendon xanthomas frequently contain cholesterol clefts and fibrosis.2Certain xanthomas have been associated with specific underlying lipoprotein disorders, giving them diagnostic utility.1 FD is a rare disorder characterized by elevated plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels.1,3Most cases are associated withAPOE-ε2homozygosity, transmitted in an autosomal recessive mode with variable penetrance.4Adult-onset tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are characteristic of FD.3Planar xanthomas in the palmar creases, known as xanthoma striatum palmare (Figure 2), are seen in 20% of FD cases and are pathognomonic.3,5In the present case, the coexistence of these xanthoma types allowed the diagnosis of FD to be essentially ensured before obtaining confirmatory lipid profiling. By appreciating xanthomas as diagnostic clues, dermatologists can help recognize underlying FD. This is critical given that FD is associated with a substantial increased risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease if untreated.3Treatment includes lipid- and cholesterol-lowering agents that mitigate cardiovascular risk and often induces full xanthoma regression.3 Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH), an autosomal dominant disorder associated with defects in genes affecting the low-density lipoprotein−receptor pathway, is also characterized by elevated plasma cholesterol and xanthoma formation.3,4However, FH has normal triglyceride levels and distinct characteristic xanthomas. Tendon xanthomas, often involving the Achilles tendon and extensor tendons of the digits, and corneal arcus before age 45 years, are highly specific findings for FH, whereas tuberous and tuberoeruptive xanthomas are much less common.1,3,6Intertriginous planar xanthomas, typically in the interdigital webspaces, are pathognomonic for homozygous FH.1,3,7If xanthomas develop, they usually appear after the third decade of life in heterozygotes and as early as the first decade in homozygotes.6,7 Another genetic disorder to consider is familial hyperchylomicronemia syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder associated with variations in lipoprotein lipase; however, unlike FD, it is associated with transient eruptive xanthomas and very elevated plasma triglycerides.8Lastly, sitosterolemia (ie, phytosterolemia or xenosterolemia) is an autosomal recessive disorder (caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous variants inABCG5/ABCG8genes) in which the body accumulates excess plant sterols.9This disorder shares several clinical features with other inherited lipid disorders, including xanthoma formation and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease,3,9and could be considered but it would be dismissed through laboratory and clinical assessments. Similar to FH and in contrast to FD, patients often present early in life with tendon xanthomas.9What distinguishes sitosterolemia from FH, FD, and other lipoprotein disorders is the presence of markedly elevated plasma levels of plant sterols3,9; these patients may have elevated total cholesterol levels, but a standard lipid panel does not provide specific diagnostic information.9

A shave biopsy specimen was taken from a papule on the elbow and sent for histopathologic analysis (Figure 1B). A fasting serum lipid panel was also obtained. Based on the clinical, histologic, and laboratory findings, the patient was diagnosed with an underlying genetic disorder.
